quote: Man wird da wahrscheinlich finden, dass [-a-] auch nur algebraische Singularitäten im Endlichen auftreten dürfen, aber nicht blos Pole [-...-] wie bei den linearen, sondern auch Verzweigungspunkte
english: One will probably find there that only algebraic singularities may occur in the finite region as well, but not merely poles as in the linear case, rather also branch points.
topic: Hilbert plans to extend the parameter-expansion method from linear to higher-degree (nonlinear) differential equations and expects algebraic singularities including branch points, with examples y''=λy² and Δu=λu². He then begins constructing a function f(n) satisfying an infinite chain of iterated-logarithm limit equations, attributed to Franz Meyer.

triage.modern_statement: Take a nonlinear boundary-value problem that depends on a parameter λ, for example y'' = λy² or Δu = λu² with fixed boundary data. Expand its solution as a power series in λ, as Hilbert had done for linear problems, and continue it analytically in the complex λ-plane. In the linear (Fredholm) case the solution is a meromorphic function of λ, so its only finite singularities are poles at eigenvalues. Hilbert's conjecture: in the nonlinear case the solution branches are still algebroid in λ. Their only finite singularities would be algebraic ones, meaning poles and also algebraic branch points (Puiseux-type) where several solution branches meet. In modern language this is the local structure of solution sets of analytic nonlinear Fredholm equations F(u,λ)=0 near bifurcation and turning points.
triage.answered_by: The local version was answered by Hilbert's student Erhard Schmidt in 1908, building on A. M. Lyapunov (1906). In 'Zur Theorie der linearen und nichtlinearen Integralgleichungen. III. Teil: Über die Auflösung der nichtlinearen Integralgleichung und die Verzweigung ihrer Lösungen' (Math. Ann. 65, 1908, pp. 370–399), Schmidt reduced nonlinear integral equations (and so boundary-value problems) to a finite system of analytic 'branching equations'. Near a critical λ these behave like algebraic equations, with algebraic branch points. This is now called Lyapunov–Schmidt reduction. I found no source showing that the stronger global claim (no non-algebraic singularities anywhere in the finite λ-plane) was proved as a general theorem.

evidence.claim: Schmidt's 1908 Math. Ann. 65 paper (pp. 370–399) deals with solving the nonlinear integral equation and with the branching (Verzweigung) of its solutions. A historical survey of nonlinear integral equations covering Hilbert, Schmidt, Lalescu and Bratu cites it as a key follow-up to Hilbert.
The Lyapunov–Schmidt method for branching of solutions of nonlinear equations goes back to Lyapunov (1906) and Schmidt (1908).
Work on branching of solutions of nonlinear operator equations near branch points, using reduction to finite-dimensional branching equations, still continues.
The survey also discusses Bratu's nonlinear integral equations (1910, 1914), which lead to the Bratu/Gelfand-type problems related to Δu = λf(u).

triage.why: The note is a programme from Hilbert's diary: extend the parameter-expansion method of his integral-equation theory to nonlinear equations, and expect branch points as well as poles. This is not one of the 23 problems or the 24th problem. It was taken up almost at once inside Hilbert's school. Schmidt's 1908 Math. Ann. paper explicitly treats the branching of solutions of nonlinear integral equations, and, together with Lyapunov's 1906 work, it established the expected algebraic branch-point behaviour near critical parameter values. Branching theory (Lyapunov–Schmidt reduction, bifurcation theory, including Bratu/Gelfand-type problems) is still an active research field. Confidence is low for three reasons. First, the link between this diary entry and Schmidt's paper is my own inference; no source I found connects them directly. Second, I did not find a source proving the global claim that only algebraic singularities occur in the whole finite λ-plane. Third, I could not read Schmidt's paper itself, so the claim that his branching equations give Puiseux-type behaviour rests on standard theory, not on these sources. So 'solved' applies to the local branching question only.
